name: EarWell infant ear molding

lead: EarWell is a non-surgical molding system placed on a newborn's ear to reshape cartilage deformities such as a folded or protruding ear. It is a pediatric medical device rather than an adult appearance product, and appears in this wiki as the non-surgical alternative to later ear surgery.

Published series from several centers, including in China and the United States, report that most treated ears improve when treatment starts early. No randomized controlled trial appears among the studies reviewed.

paras: Researchers describe newborn ear cartilage as unusually pliable during the first weeks of life, attributed to circulating maternal estrogens [2][4]. A splint holds the ear in a corrected shape during this window so that the cartilage sets in the new form.

The reviewed studies describe treatment as non-invasive, with outcomes depending strongly on how early it begins and on deformity severity [4]. Skin irritation from adhesives is a general consideration for any taped device. Individual decisions are made with a pediatric or plastic-surgery clinician.

lead: The EarWell Infant Ear Correction System is a non-surgical splinting system used to reshape congenital ear deformities in newborns, such as constricted (lop) ears, Stahl's ear and prominent ears. It is a molding approach in which a shaped device is adhered to the infant ear for a period of weeks [1][2].

Proponents among the plastic surgeons who developed and report on it say that the cartilage of a newborn is unusually plastic because of maternal estrogens, so molding begun in the first days or weeks of life can correct deformities that would otherwise be addressed by otoplasty later [3][4].

Published evidence consists mostly of single-center prospective and retrospective series, with correction rates generally reported as high when treatment starts early [1][4][5]. No randomized controlled trial is listed among the studies reviewed here.
infobox: Early infancy, ideally the first weeks of life [3]

paras: The system is designed to shape several parts of the ear, including the antihelix, the triangular fossa, the helical rim and an overly prominent conchal-mastoid angle [1]. Its developers describe it as an evolution from earlier approaches that used tapes, glues and stents [1].
Reported conditions treated include constricted ear malformations, for which one practice proposed a severity classification based on anatomical findings [2].

Authors of one study state that around one-third of infants have ear anomalies and fewer than one-third of those correct on their own [4]. They and others attribute the window for molding to circulating maternal estrogens that keep auricular cartilage pliable [3][4].
A 2015 study hypothesized that starting treatment in the first days of life with a more rigid system would shorten treatment time and raise correction rates [3].

A single-physician review of 831 infant ear deformities in 488 patients described the development of the system and the range of deformities treated [1]. A retrospective review of consecutive infants treated from 2011 to 2014 reported outcomes and proposed the classification of constricted ears [2].

A single-center prospective study over three years assessed efficacy and the factors that affect outcome [4]. Studies from China examined treatment efficiency and long-term effectiveness [6][5], and a study compared two molding systems [7]. A one-year outcomes study focused on constricted ears [8], and a review article summarized molding for congenital auricular deformities [9]. An anthropometric study characterized congenital auricular deformities in newborns [10].
The abstracts available for these studies do not describe randomized, blinded comparisons against no treatment, and several are retrospective or from a single center.
